D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Unemployed farm families and veterans have gathered in the towns of Shanxi. Republican organizers are calling on local schools and former army comrades to demand an inquiry into land distribution and relief. Several garrisons have joined the assemblies, and provincial officials have asked the court to decide on their demands for compensation and the dismissal of local officers.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Veterans, local scholars and dispossessed farmers in Shanxi have gathered over the hardship and arrests that followed the land surveys. Republican organisers use village schools and old military connections to circulate petitions, calling on each county to choose delegates and hold officers accountable for the seizure of farmland.\n\nSeveral garrisons refuse to surrender the accused officers and have turned away the governor's investigators. The county delegates demand the removal of the chief commissioner, a fresh review of titles and compensation for the injured farmers. Republican organisers are seeking allies among the troops and preparing to rise if their petitions fail. The Ministry of Justice has referred the case to the court: dismiss the officials and reopen the inquiry, or prosecute the assemblies for defying the law.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Order the garrisons to surrender their records and punish those who defy the law.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Land commissioners in [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_mess_imprisonment_state').GetName] have arrested villagers who drafted petitions over disputed titles and placed them in military custody for concealing property. Officers widened the arrests to local gentry, teachers and clerks who kept the old deeds.\n\nThe new law empowers officials to settle land ownership, but also permits farmers to defend their property. The prisoners' families have taken their deeds to the provincial capital, and the governor has referred the case to the Ministry of Justice. The commissioners warn of collusion and unrest and ask the Ministry of War to protect the officers involved. Transferring a few officials would allow the affair to pass quietly. A prosecution would make the reform's own agents answer for crimes committed in its name.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Manufacturers and merchants in [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_industrialists_support_state').GetName] have jointly offered to finance land reform. Workshops are expanding and more carts travel the commercial roads. They want the new law to allow farming families to move freely and bring more workers into the towns.\n\nTheir representatives also seek to submit proposals on land, roads and employment contracts through the Consultative Council. The governor is willing to accept the funding. Officials in the Ministry of Revenue argue that these wealthy men understand industry and could take a greater part in government. The rising manufacturers hope to gain a position in imperial affairs commensurate with their wealth.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: Rural families are arriving in [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_peasants_in_city_state').GetName] to seek wages. Employers have asked the authorities to uphold the current recruitment arrangements.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The streets of [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_peasants_in_city_state').GetName] are filling with newcomers from the countryside. Farming families have sold their land and come in search of wages. Employment brokers send them to factories and building sites, deducting recruitment and lodging charges from their pay.\n\nWorkers have accused the brokers of withholding contracts and enforcing old debts. Manufacturers fear that an inquiry will disrupt recruitment, while local gentry defend brokers linked to their own associations. The governor must decide whether to prosecute the organisations that bind workers to them or leave the disputes to ordinary civil proceedings. In these growing towns, the promise that peasants could leave their old estates and freely earn a living faces its first practical tests.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.before: The Great Revolution has passed, but its promises still guide clerks, junior officers, soldiers and peasants. They see the land revolution as the continuation of an unfinished cause.\n\nThe Empire is not the republic envisioned by the young scholars and soldiers of 1810. Republican exiles in the south and northwest call Mu Zhongtang a traitor. Yet many still regard him and his companions as heirs of the Enlightenment movement and champions of progress. Their enthusiasm sustains the reform, even as each new demand tests their patience.
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The fires of the Great Revolution have faded, but its promises still guide clerks, junior officers, soldiers and peasants seeking release from old obligations. They see the land revolution as the continuation of an unfinished cause.\n\nAfter Mu Zhongtang became emperor, the Six Ministries administered the state, while founding commanders and senior ministers in the Senate monopolised legislative power. The Consultative Council gathers petitions and makes proposals whose fate rests with those who govern. Republican exiles in the south and northwest call Mu a traitor. Many supporters of reform still regard him and his companions as champions of enlightenment and progress. Imperial policy depends on the surviving enthusiasm of these officials, soldiers and farmers. Each new survey, change of occupation and reorganisation of the estates asks them to endure more.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The imperial government has fallen. The republicans have taken over its provinces and offices and established the Han Commonwealth. D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Since 1444, the Qin military colonies of Northern Ming have developed into an estate system across the north. Governors charged with enforcing the law may lack the force to compel their garrisons, while the founding commanders in the Senate are reluctant to surrender their own property. The provinces can proceed separately and suspend reform where disputes become unmanageable. New revenue and production must eventually replace the army's landed income.

Land commissioners in [SCOPE.sState('nesnd_land_petition_state').GetName] have surveyed the countryside under the new law, yet several local military estates still collect rent under the old rules. Farmers who have paid the redemption price are told by their old masters that their fields remain military property and that the dues must be paid. Teachers who helped draft their petitions have been arrested for concealing property.\n\nThe deeds submitted by the affected counties contradict the garrison registers. As the dispute drags on, farmers gather in the county towns, awaiting an answer from the government that promised to free them.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: This movement began with the Western Qin Great Revolution of 1810. People of the age understood it as a modern economic transformation arising among the agrarian states of the East, where powerful lineages had long dominated rural life. Through purchase or compulsory confiscation, land accumulated beyond all measure by its old owners was redistributed among a portion of the peasantry. The aim was to break the lineages’ hold over the rural population. The ruling group of the Empire of China suspended the movement during its rise to power. Around Mu Zhongtang’s southern campaign of 1820, however, he and his confidants revived it to restore the economy, free productive activity and mobilise peasants and soldiers.

我们完善的土地法案、雇工法案、民法家庭相关条文已被推行至帝国的每一个角落，建起来一个崭新的经济秩序。在这一秩序中，我们解放了被血亲家族束缚了数千年的人们。高高的田垄回归了它自然资源的本来面目。

随着旧宗族和土地不再能锁住农民，无数稚嫩、满是灰土却充满朝气的脸孔源源不断地从郊野涌入城市。他们憧憬新的生活。一种用人类的智慧和科学力量构建的生活。许多血缘的余孽用各种各样的地方团体伪装自己，试图重新夺回对这些人的控制。但巡捕的警棍和判官的惊堂木终会粉碎他们的野心。

我们又一次将开国帝牧仲棠的理想照进现实。我们证明了这个帝国是为了华夏民族之利益而构建。为此，它将保护哪怕最细小无助者自由选择自己命运的权力——他们如今在城市中追求幸福，给帝国带来新的繁荣。
D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after:
Our revised laws on land, employment and family relations have reached every corner of the Empire and established a new economic order. We have freed people from the bonds of kinship that held them for thousands of years. The fields have returned to their proper place as a natural resource.

As the old lineages and their land can no longer bind the peasantry, young faces, dusty yet full of life, stream from the countryside into the cities. They dream of a new life built through human intelligence and science. The remnants of hereditary power disguise themselves as local associations and try to regain control over them. Police batons and the magistrate’s gavel will break their ambitions.

Once more we have brought the founding emperor Mu Zhongtang’s ideals into reality. We have shown that this Empire was built for the interests of the Huaxia nation. It will protect even the weakest person’s freedom to choose a future. Those now seeking happiness in the cities are bringing new prosperity to the Empire.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The streets of [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_peasants_in_city_state').GetName] are filling with newcomers from the countryside. Farming families have sold their land and come in search of wages. Employment brokers send them to factories and building sites, deducting recruitment and lodging charges from their pay.\n\nWorkers have accused the brokers of withholding contracts and enforcing old debts. Manufacturers fear that an inquiry will disrupt recruitment, while local gentry defend brokers linked to their own associations. The governor must decide whether to prosecute the organisations that bind workers to them or leave the disputes to ordinary civil proceedings. In these growing towns, the promise that peasants could leave their old estates and freely earn a living faces its first practical tests.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: The fires of the Great Revolution have faded, but its promises still guide clerks, junior officers, soldiers and peasants seeking release from old obligations. They see the land revolution as the continuation of an unfinished cause.\n\nAfter Mu Zhongtang became emperor, the Six Ministries administered the state, while founding commanders and senior ministers in the Senate monopolised legislative power. The Consultative Council gathers petitions and makes proposals whose fate rests with those who govern. Republican exiles in the south and northwest call Mu a traitor. Many supporters of reform still regard him and his companions as champions of enlightenment and progress. Imperial policy depends on the surviving enthusiasm of these officials, soldiers and farmers. Each new survey, change of occupation and reorganisation of the estates asks them to endure more.

D:\\Users\\Eric Liu\\Documents\\Paradox.after: Since 1444, the Qin military colonies of Northern Ming have developed into an estate system across the north. Land supplied the army's food and pay, while the army sustained taxation and conquest. Military and agricultural interests grew together. Bringing these lands and mines into civilian use now threatens entrenched military privileges.\n\nThe Ministry of Revenue wants the estates brought under ordinary taxation and management. The Ministry of War must answer officers who invoke unpaid wages and past service. Governors charged with enforcing the law may lack the force to compel their garrisons, while the founding commanders in the Senate are reluctant to surrender their own property. The provinces can proceed separately and suspend reform where disputes become unmanageable. New revenue and production must eventually replace the army's landed income.

Land commissioners in [SCOPE.sState('nesnd_land_petition_state').GetName] have surveyed the countryside under the new law, yet several local military estates still collect rent under the old rules. Farmers who have paid the redemption price are told by their old masters that their fields remain military property and that the dues must be paid. Teachers who helped draft their petitions have been arrested for concealing property.\n\nThe deeds submitted by the affected counties contradict the garrison registers. The provincial governor seeks authority to review the cases, while the commissioners ask the court to send troops to recover the withheld records. As the dispute drags on, farmers gather in the county towns, awaiting an answer from the government that promised to free them.
